cards.html: This guide is for a developer who can build a web app and now has to decide how people log in, stay logged in, get back in after forgetting a password, and what each person may see. It assumes Python, HTTP, and the basics of salted hashing and session cookies, but no prior auth design experience.

The running example is Rankwise, a plain-JavaScript progressive web app (PWA) served by FastAPI on a Mac over home Wi-Fi, with two learners, Taha and Batul, today and perhaps thousands of public users later. Most auth decisions differ between those two worlds; the guide shows how to reason about both. Each chapter ends with pitfalls, a decision guide and key takeaways; code is Python 3.10+, and anything labelled "the wrong way" is followed by the fix.

ChapterWhat you will learnMinutes
1. The mental modelThe vocabulary, the account lifecycle, threat modelling, trust boundaries, recurring principles10
2. Storing passwordsArgon2id, salts, peppers, parameters, rehashing, migration, NIST password policy, breached-password checks15
3. The login flow end to endUsers table, sign-up, login, logout, enumeration, rate limiting, logging, a complete FastAPI example18
4. Sessions and tokensServer-side sessions, cookie attributes, CSRF, XSS, JWT, refresh rotation, when to use which20
5. Forgot password and account recoveryReset tokens done right, email verification, magic links, recovery codes, recovery without email13
6. Other ways to log inOAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, Google sign-in, passkeys, TOTP, PINs17
7. AuthorisationOwnership checks, IDOR, RBAC/ABAC/ReBAC, policy functions, admin impersonation, row-level security12
8. Build vs buyDIY versus Supabase, Firebase, Auth0, Clerk, Cognito, Keycloak, and a decision framework13

ChapterWhat you will learnMinutes
9. What can go wrongOver 20 failure scenarios and an incident response checklist15
10. Scaling and operationsCost model, capacity numbers, multi-server sessions, secret rotation, monitoring, GDPR, testing12
11. Worked design: RankwiseA two-phase design for the example app, with data model, endpoints and plan12
12. Self-check, glossary and further readingQuestions with answers, 40+ terms, authoritative sources10

Total: roughly two and a half to three hours at a steady pace.

"I need to ship login this week." Read chapter 2 (sections on Argon2id and password policy), chapter 3 in full, chapter 4 up to and including CSRF, and chapter 7's section on ownership checks. Then skim the catalogue in chapter 9. About an hour.

"I want to design auth systems myself." Read everything in order. Chapters 1, 4, 6 and 8 hold most of the judgement. Finish with the self-check in chapter 12.

"I am deciding whether to use a hosted provider." Read chapter 1, chapter 8, then chapter 11's phase 2. Then chapters 4 and 7: a provider handles login, not your API's sessions and authorisation.

"I only care about Rankwise." Read chapter 11 first and follow its cross-references.

cards.s: What you will be able to do afterwards
cards.html:
• Explain why an auth design is safe or unsafe, and what it defends against.
  • Implement password login, server-side sessions, password reset and ownership checks in FastAPI without copying code you do not understand.
  • Choose between sessions and JWTs, building and buying, and passwords, passkeys and social login, based on your conditions.
  • Spot common failures in review, and know what to do in the first hour of an incident.
